entries_new.name: Rason Special Economic Zone
aka: Rajin-Sonbong Free Economic and Trade Zone
entries_new.laws: Law on the Rason Economic and Trade Zone (1993, amended six times to 2011); 16 regulations in the 2016 collection
entries_new.story:
The Rason Special Economic Zone is a 746 square kilometre zone in the far north-east of North Korea, on the Tumen River border with China and Russia. North Korea founded it as the Rajin Free Economic and Trade Zone in December 1991 and expanded it as the Rajin-Sonbong zone in September 1993, to draw foreign investment and pilot market economics in a controlled area. Foreign currency may be used in the zone, and foreign companies must be invited by the Committee for Promotion of External Economic Cooperation, which runs it.
Its law has been amended six times, most recently on 3 December 2011, and a 2016 collection holds 16 regulations on matters such as labour and tax for foreign-invested firms. By the end of 1996, 51 foreign businesses had invested US$37.3 million. Chinese and Russian companies have invested, and Mongolia joined in about 2013. North Korean Economy Watch reports a 56 kilometre electrified fence around it.

entries_new.name: Kaesong Industrial Region
entries_new.founder: Governments of North and South Korea; Hyundai Asan
entries_new.pop: About 53,000 North Korean workers and 800 South Korean staff (April 2013)
entries_new.challenge: Closed by South Korea in February 2016; North Korea expelled South Korean workers and froze assets
entries_new.story:
The Kaesong Industrial Region is a special administrative industrial region of North Korea, formed in 2002 from part of Kaesong city, ten kilometres north of the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Its industrial park, opened in December 2004, was run by a South Korean committee under a 50-year lease from 2004, with Hyundai Asan hired to develop the land. South Korean firms employed North Korean workers there: 123 companies employed about 53,000 North Korean workers and 800 South Korean staff as of April 2013.
North Korea withdrew its workers in April 2013 during a crisis, and the park reopened after an agreement that August. On 10 February 2016 South Korea's Ministry of Unification closed it, which it called temporary, after a North Korean satellite launch and claimed hydrogen bomb test. North Korea then expelled the South Korean workers and froze their assets. In 2017 President Moon Jae-in said he wanted to reopen and expand it.

entries_new.story: Thilawa Special Economic Zone is a 2,500 hectare zone being developed in Kyauktan and Thanlyin Townships, 25 kilometres south of Yangon, Myanmar. It was announced in January 2011. On 29 October 2013 the Myanmar and Japanese governments set up a consortium to develop it, including Japan Thilawa SEZ Company, backed by Mitsubishi, Marubeni and Sumitomo, Myanmar Thilawa SEZ Holdings, a management committee and the Japan International Cooperation Agency. Construction of the $3.28 billion project began in May 2014, and the first phase opened at the end of September 2015. A 2007 Xinhua report listed Thilawa Port among six planned free trade zones.
